reference.source: Apley & Solomon / standard sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: Sciatica describes radicular leg pain following a dermatomal distribution below the knee, often with associated tingling, numbness, or weakness, and typically worse than any back pain
The commonest cause is compression or irritation of a lumbosacral nerve root by a prolapsed intervertebral disc, most often at L4-5 or L5-S1
In older patients, lumbar spinal stenosis causing neurogenic claudication is a frequent cause, with leg symptoms brought on by walking and relieved by sitting or flexion
A positive straight-leg raise (and crossed straight-leg raise) suggests lower lumbar nerve root tension, while the femoral stretch test targets higher roots
Examination should localise the affected root through its characteristic sensory, motor, and reflex changes
Most disc-related sciatica improves over weeks to a few months with conservative care, staying active, analgesia by principle, and physiotherapy
MRI is reserved for severe or persistent symptoms, progressive deficit, or when surgery or injection is being considered, not for routine early management
Surgery such as discectomy is considered for persistent disabling radicular pain that fails conservative treatment, or urgently for significant or progressive neurological deficit
Screen every patient for cauda equina and other red flags at presentation and again if symptoms change
reference.pathophysiology: Sciatica is caused by compression, tension, or chemical irritation of a lumbosacral nerve root, most commonly from a herniated disc whose nucleus material both mechanically compresses and inflames the root. Other causes include degenerative foraminal or central canal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, and less often tumour or infection. Nerve root inflammation and ischaemia generate the characteristic radiating pain and neurological signs in the corresponding dermatome and myotome.
additionalDifferentials: Lumbar spinal or foraminal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
Piriformis syndrome or deep gluteal syndrome
Peripheral neuropathy or nerve entrapment (e.g. peroneal nerve)
Hip or sacroiliac joint pathology referring to the leg
Spinal tumour or infection compressing a nerve root
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis with root localisation; imaging not required for typical early sciatica without red flags
MRI of the lumbar spine for severe, persistent, or progressive symptoms or when intervention is planned
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography in selected cases to clarify the level or exclude peripheral neuropathy
Blood tests and targeted imaging if infection or malignancy is suspected
redFlags: Cauda equina syndrome: saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence, and bilateral or progressive leg weakness requiring emergency imaging and decompression
Progressive or severe motor deficit such as foot drop needing urgent assessment
Features suggesting malignancy: previous cancer, unexplained weight loss, age over 50, and night pain
Features suggesting infection: fever, immunosuppression, intravenous drug use, and severe unremitting pain
reference.prognosis: The majority of disc-related cases resolve within six to twelve weeks with conservative treatment, but a proportion have persistent or recurrent symptoms; surgery gives faster relief of leg pain in selected patients, and outcomes worsen if significant neurological deficit is not treated promptly.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about and detect cauda equina features, risking permanent deficit
Ordering early MRI and over-attributing symptoms to incidental disc findings
Mistaking peripheral entrapment, hip, or vascular pathology for radicular pain
Delaying referral for progressive motor deficit
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Reassure and encourage staying active, since most disc-related sciatica settles over weeks to a few months with conservative care
Provide analgesia and structured physiotherapy while avoiding prolonged bed rest
Consider a fluoroscopically guided epidural or transforaminal corticosteroid injection for severe, persistent radicular pain
Reserve MRI of the lumbar spine for severe, progressive or persistent symptoms or when intervention is planned
Refer for surgical decompression such as microdiscectomy in selected patients with persistent disabling pain or significant neurological deficit
Escalate urgently for suspected cauda equina syndrome or progressive motor deficit, with emergency imaging and surgical decompression
Manage neurogenic claudication from spinal stenosis in older patients with physiotherapy, activity modification and decompressive surgery where disabling
